The river had fallen overnight, leaving a brown ribbon along the footbridge supports. Mara carried a box of brushes from the workshop to the bank. The council had sent paint in three different tins, none quite the color of the surviving rail. A sketch by Ellis showed the bridge before the upstream steps were added, when the path ended at a narrow patch of gravel.

“We should start where the boards are dry,” Mara said. She placed the brushes beneath the shelter of the first arch. The work could begin without waiting for the sun to reach the center span. On the far bank, a bicycle lay beside the reeds. Its owner was nowhere in sight, and the front wheel turned whenever the breeze crossed the water.

Jonah brought the first tin from the workshop. He stirred the paint with a clean strip of wood. “This will be lighter when it dries,” Jonah replied. The old rail was darker underneath, where hands had worn away the surface. A careful patch might look strange for a week and then disappear into the rest. Mara tested a brush on the inside of a post.

The morning widened around the slow task. A pair of ducks passed beneath the bridge and disappeared behind a fallen branch. Footsteps sounded on the path above the bank. Niko arrived with a paper bag of bread and left it on the dry steps. They watched the trial patch without touching it. “The middle tin looks closer,” Niko said.

Mara compared the lids in the sunlight. “We can use that one for the top rail,” Mara replied. The brushes would need separate cloths if the colors were to stay clean. Jonah moved the first tin into the shade, keeping its lid nearby. Niko folded the empty paper bag into a tray for the smaller tools.

Near noon, Saira came down the upstream path carrying the missing bicycle pump. She stopped beside the reeds. “I can take the lower rail after lunch,” Saira said. The offer gave the afternoon a different shape. Mara found another brush in the box and set it beside the folded tray. Across the river, the new patch had begun to dry, holding a little of the morning light against the old wood.
